subject: Business Models
title: Antitrust and Platforms
description: A quick win: understand Antitrust and Platforms.

hook.text: The EU fined Google $8.2 billion across three antitrust cases. The biggest tech penalties in history.

buildup.text: Antitrust law was built for industrial monopolies. Platform monopolies don't fit neatly into old frameworks.

discovery.text: Platforms often offer free or cheap products. Traditional antitrust focuses on high prices as consumer harm.

twist.text: The harm may be to competition, not consumers. Amazon's low prices hurt rivals more than customers.

climax.text: Regulators worldwide are rewriting rules. The EU's Digital Markets Act specifically targets platform gatekeepers.

punchline.text: Free products, massive power. Old antitrust law didn't see this coming.

quiz.question: Why don't platforms fit traditional antitrust frameworks?
options: They often offer free/cheap products despite having monopoly power

details.summary: Antitrust enforcement increasingly targets dominant platforms for anti-competitive behavior including self-preferencing, killer acquisitions, and exclusionary practices. Traditional antitrust frameworks struggle to address platform power that stems from network effects rather than pricing.
details.whyItMatters: Regulation is reshaping platform economics. Antitrust actions against Google, Apple, Amazon, and Meta threaten to break up integrated ecosystems, force interoperability, and limit acquisitions that have been central to platform growth strategies.
takeaways: Dominant platforms face scrutiny for self-preferencing and exclusionary conduct
Traditional antitrust tools struggle with free products and network-based power
New regulations like the DMA aim to constrain gatekeeper platform behavior

faq.question: Why do traditional antitrust tools struggle with platform monopolies?
faq.answer: Traditional antitrust focuses on consumer harm measured by price increases. Platforms often offer free products while extracting value from attention or data. Network effects make monopoly the natural market outcome, not the result of anti-competitive behavior.

faq.question: What remedies are regulators pursuing against dominant platforms?
faq.answer: Forced interoperability, prohibition of self-preferencing in search results or app stores, restrictions on acquiring potential competitors, data portability requirements, and in extreme cases structural separation of platform divisions into independent companies.
